absent: Numeric values of tick interval, deadline sentinel, capability and state codes, and error numbers.
Registration, selection, and programming primitives for broadcast and local event devices.
Complete layouts of tick, clock event, timekeeper, migration, and timer base structures beyond referenced fields.
Lock ordering with scheduler, RCU, IRQ, and timekeeper locks outside the shown acquisitions.

findings.text: Provides CPU membership control for timer broadcast during power transitions. Caller requests forced, enabled, or disabled handling; implementation updates persistent enabled and active sets, conditionally quiesces or restores the local event source, and starts or stops the shared broadcast source when the active set transitions between empty and non-empty, honouring a sticky forced flag and distinguishing periodic from single-shot global modes.

Defines broadcast lifecycle operations. Suspend quiesces the shared broadcast source when present. Initialization reserves the global active, enabled, scratch, and, when single-shot operation is configured, the single-shot, pending, and forced CPU sets.

Exposes single-shot broadcast state and hotplug repair. One accessor returns the set of CPUs currently delegated to the broadcast source. A non-instrumented predicate reports whether the calling CPU has a forced broadcast pending. A per-CPU fixup ensures a delegated CPU whose tick layer has entered single-shot mode also places its local event source in the corresponding state. A hotplug helper reassigns broadcast ownership away from a departing CPU and repairs a pending forced expiry on the survivor.

Controls entry to and exit from deep idle under single-shot broadcast. The full variant first attempts a dedicated per-CPU wakeup source and, if unavailable, falls back to shared broadcast management, refusing idle when no broadcast path exists. A reduced variant only vetoes idle when no broadcast source exists or when the source is timer-queue based. Exit restores local handling and either suppresses reprogramming when expiry will arrive via broadcast or re-arms the local source.

Periodic broadcast reception clears a forced reprogram marker, ignores events when the shared source is quiesced, distributes expiry to online delegated CPUs, advances a single-shot shared source by one tick interval when applicable, and invokes local tick handling only after releasing the broadcast lock.

Single-shot broadcast reception resets the shared deadline, samples current time, partitions delegated CPUs into expired and future sets, records expired remote CPUs as pending, merges and clears forced requests, restricts delivery to online CPUs, wakes expired CPUs, re-arms the shared source to the earliest future deadline when one remains, and runs local handling after unlocking.

Broadcast dispatch removes the handling CPU from the target set, decides local delivery based on whether the shared source is backed by the high-resolution timer queue, and otherwise delegates remote wakeup to the broadcast operation advertised by the first target CPU device. Periodic dispatch targets the intersection of online and delegated CPUs. Timer-queue backing suppresses direct local handling to avoid re-entrant expiry processing, and ownership by a specific CPU vetoes that CPU entering deep idle.

Tick and broadcast operation moves between periodic and single-shot modes. Local event sources move among quiesced, single-shot, and stopped single-shot conditions. Broadcast membership moves among unlisted, enabled, and forced states via force, enable, disable, enter, and exit requests, with forced membership persisting across disable until explicitly cleared and with periodic global mode short-circuiting single-shot entry.

All mutations of broadcast membership sets, shared source mode and deadlines, and local source quiesce or re-arm during broadcast transitions occur while holding the broadcast raw spin lock, using interrupt-saving acquisition in control, suspend, and hotplug contexts and plain acquisition in interrupt handling contexts. Local tick handlers run after release to avoid deadlock when switching modes.

Global tick count and next period updates occur under the jiffies raw lock with sequence protection for readers. Timekeeper progression holds the core timekeeper lock with interrupts saved. Auxiliary timekeepers are visited with a lockless activity precheck followed by per-instance locking and a validity gate. Jiffies readers use sequence retry to obtain a consistent count and monotonic base.

Per-CPU tick state combines a mode selector with a reference to the CPU local event source. The shared broadcast holder combines a mode selector with a reference to the active broadcast event source. Event sources expose capability flags, a pending deadline, a forced reprogram marker, an ownership binding, a remote wakeup operation, and a local expiry callback. Broadcast CPU sets comprise active periodic, enabled, scratch, single-shot, pending, and forced sets.

Global tick progression state includes a monotonic next-period instant, a tick counter, and a designated CPU selector with a boot-time sentinel. Timer migration per-CPU state includes availability, grouping, group mask, idle flag, wakeup instant, and a consistency lock with a walk descriptor carrying current time, child mask, earliest expiry, and a decision flag. Timer bases expose a next-expiry hint that remote writers update with ordered stores.

Periodic tick handling on the designated CPU advances the next-period instant and tick count, refreshes load tracking, and advances wall time including auxiliary keepers. Every CPU then accounts the tick to the current task, runs expired high-resolution queues and timer bases, notifies scheduler and RCU and optional subsystems, and raises timer soft processing when a base deadline has passed or remote migration work is required.

Maximum deadline value denotes absence of a pending event. Auxiliary progression is a no-op when unconfigured and otherwise advances only valid instances among the active set. Periodic tick advancement applies only on the designated CPU. Timer migration availability requires both group association and an available flag; active CPUs decide remote handling by hierarchy walk while idle CPUs compare current time against a wakeup instant with word-size-dependent locking.

Failure to distribute a tick is reported once as critical with possible unresponsive CPUs. Re-entrant expiry occurs if timer-queue-backed broadcast runs local handling inline, so local delivery is suppressed in that case. Holding the broadcast lock across local handling can deadlock during mode switch. Broadcasting to offline CPUs is warned and clamped. Missed remote expiry updates can delay a timer by one tick or cause spurious soft processing. Expired local deadlines during exit are deferred through the forced set to avoid reprogram ping-pong and starvation.

Facts observed include interval TICK_NSEC, sentinel KTIME_MAX, capabilities CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP and CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER, states CLOCK_EVT_STATE_SHUTDOWN and CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT and CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT_STOPPED, modes TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC and TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT, controls TICK_BROADCAST_FORCE and TICK_BROADCAST_ON and TICK_BROADCAST_OFF with enter and exit selectors, boot marker TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT, and negative outcomes for busy, invalid argument, and missing device.
